topic.title: The gym is built for people who won't come
topic.claim: Gyms push the annual plan hard because their business works best if most of the members who paid never show up.
topic.moment: The trainer says 'one year is basically half price' and you sign up on January 3rd feeling like a new person.

turn.believed: The yearly plan is a discount for committed people.
turn.actually: It's money paid upfront by people the gym expects to stop coming.

topic.feeling: Guilty every time I pass the gym, and they're happy I feel that way.
topic.villain: Upfront annual memberships sold on future motivation.
topic.because: A gym can only fit so many people. It sells far more memberships than it has space for, betting that most won't come.
topic.payoff: Pay monthly for three months. If you still go, the annual plan is a discount. If not, you just saved nine months.
topic.behaviour: Gyms offer steep annual discounts and push hardest in January and after Diwali.
topic.mechanism: Upfront money from members who drop off pays for the few who stay.
topic.group: Young working people trying to get fit
topic.send_to: The friend who has paid for a gym membership for the last three years in a row.
topic.why_now: Wellness spending is up, and annual plans are being pushed harder than ever.

score.why: The annual gym plan is money from people the gym expects to stop coming. The trap is the guilt you feel at the gate.

mechanism.broken_premise: None of the premises is false. One needs a caveat. Premise 3 says monthly payers 'must be won back every month', but most monthly plans renew automatically. DellaVigna & Malmendier found that monthly members pay more per visit than a pay-per-visit pass would cost and stay enrolled longer than annual members. So people who stop coming but keep paying monthly also fund the regulars. Upfront annual payment makes that subsidy bigger, but it isn't the only way it happens.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Mass-market gyms set their membership numbers and prices on the expectation that most members will rarely or never come. Planet Fitness has averaged about 6,500 members per gym when most of its clubs hold around 300 people, so people who pay and stay home cover the cost of space and equipment the regulars use. Annual prepaid plans make the gym's take even more certain because it gets the whole year's money on day one. Monthly plans that renew automatically have the same effect, since people put off cancelling. The take holds: the cheaper price depends on people not showing up. One exception is that some independent gyms cap membership so they never sell more than they can hold.

[cover] Your gym's annual plan is a [bet that you'll stop coming]
The discount is real. So is the reason they can afford it.
 

[slide 1] Your gym's annual plan isn't a discount for committed people. It's a bet that you'll stop coming.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] January 3rd. The trainer walks you past the shiny treadmills and says it. "Monthly is ₹2,500. One year is basically half price."
You pay ₹15,000. You walk out feeling like a new person already.

[slide 3] A gym chain executive says an annual member comes about 150 to 160 days out of 365. Less than half the year they paid for.
A trade report says only 15% finish their plan. The other 85% is you.

[slide 4] Because a gym only has so many racks, benches and treadmills. It sells far more memberships than it could ever fit on one floor.
That only works if most members stay home.

[slide 5] Monthly money has to win you back every month. Your ₹15,000 is banked on day one, whether you come 300 days or three.
So the members who drop off pay for the room the regulars use.

[slide 6] By March the treadmill row is half empty. Same few regulars, same machines.
Nobody from the front desk calls to ask where you went. Why would they? You already paid.

[slide 7] You bought it as the new you. The old you still logs in at 9 and sits in traffic.

[slide 8] The gym sells to the first one and banks on the second. The same report says fewer than 10% renew an annual plan. After Diwali, the offer returns.
A "Renew now" SMS lands. Your new shoes are still in the box.

[slide 9] Pay monthly for three months first.
If you're still going in April, the annual plan really is the discount. If you're not, you just saved nine months of paying for a gym you wave at from the auto.

[slide 10] You feel guilty every time you pass the gym. The gym is perfectly happy with that.

[end card] Read it again before you sign anything at a gym counter in January or after Diwali.
Send this to the friend who's bought a gym plan three Januarys in a row.

[caption] Your unused gym days aren't wasted. Someone else's membership runs on them.

[alt text] A ten-slide text post arguing that gyms push annual plans because they expect most members to stop coming. It notes that a gym-chain executive says an annual member comes about 150 to 160 days out of 365, less than half the year paid for, and that a trade report says only 15% of members finish their plan and fewer than 10% renew an annual plan. It explains that upfront money from members who drop off pays for the space the regulars use, describes the gaps in the treadmill row by March with the same regulars on their machines, and the renewal SMS after Diwali while new shoes sit in the box. It suggests paying monthly for three months before buying a yearly plan, and ends on the guilt of passing the gym, which suits the gym fine.

mechanism.broken_premise: None of the premises is false. One needs a caveat. Premise 3 says monthly payers 'must be won back every month', but most monthly plans renew automatically. DellaVigna & Malmendier found that monthly members pay more per visit than a pay-per-visit pass would cost and stay enrolled longer than annual members. So people who stop coming but keep paying monthly also fund the regulars. Upfront annual payment makes that subsidy bigger, but it isn't the only way it happens.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Mass-market gyms set their membership numbers and prices on the expectation that most members will rarely or never come. Planet Fitness has averaged about 6,500 members per gym when most of its clubs hold around 300 people, so people who pay and stay home cover the cost of space and equipment the regulars use. Annual prepaid plans make the gym's take even more certain because it gets the whole year's money on day one. Monthly plans that renew automatically have the same effect, since people put off cancelling. The take holds: the cheaper price depends on people not showing up. One exception is that some independent gyms cap membership so they never sell more than they can hold.

cover.headline: Your gym's annual plan is a [bet that you'll stop coming]
cover.sub: The discount is real. So is the reason they can afford it.

paragraphs: Your gym's annual plan isn't a discount for committed people. It's a bet that you'll stop coming.
slides.why_swipe: A bet against me? I signed up to get fit.

paragraphs: January 3rd. The trainer walks you past the shiny treadmills and says it. "Monthly is ₹2,500. One year is basically half price."
You pay ₹15,000. You walk out feeling like a new person already.
slides.why_swipe: Sounds like a good deal. What's the catch?

paragraphs: A gym chain executive says an annual member comes about 150 to 160 days out of 365. Less than half the year they paid for.
A trade report says only 15% finish their plan. The other 85% is you.
slides.why_swipe: So why would the gym want us gone?

paragraphs: Because a gym only has so many racks, benches and treadmills. It sells far more memberships than it could ever fit on one floor.
That only works if most members stay home.
slides.why_swipe: Then why push the yearly plan so hard?

paragraphs: Monthly money has to win you back every month. Your ₹15,000 is banked on day one, whether you come 300 days or three.
So the members who drop off pay for the room the regulars use.
slides.why_swipe: What does that look like from inside the gym?

paragraphs: By March the treadmill row is half empty. Same few regulars, same machines.
Nobody from the front desk calls to ask where you went. Why would they? You already paid.
slides.why_swipe: So is it my fault I stopped going?

paragraphs: You bought it as the new you. The old you still logs in at 9 and sits in traffic.
slides.why_swipe: And the gym knows which one shows up?

paragraphs: The gym sells to the first one and banks on the second. The same report says fewer than 10% renew an annual plan. After Diwali, the offer returns.
A "Renew now" SMS lands. Your new shoes are still in the box.
slides.why_swipe: So how do you beat a bet like that?

paragraphs: Pay monthly for three months first.
If you're still going in April, the annual plan really is the discount. If you're not, you just saved nine months of paying for a gym you wave at from the auto.
slides.why_swipe: And the guilt every time I pass it?

paragraphs: You feel guilty every time you pass the gym. The gym is perfectly happy with that.

end.save: Read it again before you sign anything at a gym counter in January or after Diwali.
end.send: Send this to the friend who's bought a gym plan three Januarys in a row.

draft.caption: Your unused gym days aren't wasted. Someone else's membership runs on them.
draft.alt_text: A ten-slide text post arguing that gyms push annual plans because they expect most members to stop coming. It notes that a gym-chain executive says an annual member comes about 150 to 160 days out of 365, less than half the year paid for, and that a trade report says only 15% of members finish their plan and fewer than 10% renew an annual plan. It explains that upfront money from members who drop off pays for the space the regulars use, describes the gaps in the treadmill row by March with the same regulars on their machines, and the renewal SMS after Diwali while new shoes sit in the box. It suggests paying monthly for three months before buying a yearly plan, and ends on the guilt of passing the gym, which suits the gym fine.
